🇺🇸🇵🇭🇨🇳 Balikatan 2026 Exercise Overview

During the “Balikatan 2026” exercise (April 20 – May 8), more than 17,000 troops have been deployed to Itbayat Island (Batanes Province, Philippines), where operations are being conducted under conditions максимально close to real combat. The primary focus is on scenarios involving a potential conflict in the South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait.

🔷 The main contribution comes from U.S. Armed Forces (around 10,000 personnel), alongside the Philippine military (approx. 5,000), Australia (about 400 troops), and Japan (up to 1,400 personnel). For the first time, Canada, France, and New Zealand are also participating in a full capacity.

The exercise includes live-fire drills in the waters of the South China Sea and near Taiwan, as well as coastal defense operations in northern Luzon. Despite official statements denying “training near Taiwan,” the actual geography of the maneuvers indicates preparation for a potential regional conflict.

🚚 Among the deployed systems is the U.S. Typhon (MRC) missile system, stationed in the archipelago since 2024, which previously triggered a strong reaction from China. Meanwhile, Japan plans to employ Type 88 anti-ship missiles to engage a training maritime target.

🇨🇳 A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry, Guo Jiakun, criticized the drills, stating that participating countries are “playing with fire” and contributing to rising tensions in the region. Beijing traditionally views such exercises as efforts of containment and military pressure.

🇵🇭 Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has previously noted that in the event of a conflict over Taiwan, the country would inevitably become involved due to its geographic proximity.

Overall, Balikatan 2026 reflects a shift from formal training exercises toward practical rehearsals for large-scale conflict scenarios involving U.S. allies in the Indo-Pacific.

AMLC'S ₱3.92 BILLION DATA ON VP SARA'S TRANSACTIONS DOESN'T MEAN THAT AMOUNT WAS IN HER ACCOUNT: BONG SUNTAY

The P3.92-billion figure in the AMLC report against Vice President Sara Duterte does not mean that amount was actually held in her accounts, Quezon City 4th District Rep. Bong Suntay clarified Wednesday before the House Justice Committee. 

"So it doesn't mean na 'pagka sinabi natin may 3.9 billion, does it mean na merong 3.9 billion sa loob nung account?" he asked AMLC Executive Director Atty. Ronel Buenaventura.

Buenaventura, however, stopped short of confirming or denying it, saying: "Hindi ko po... kung base lang po sa records, hindi ko pa po masabi."

Suntay pressed the AMLC chief on the figure, establishing that it reflects the total of all money movements in and out — not cash actually held. 

He walked through a hypothetical to illustrate: "Kunyari, ako, may nag-deposit sa akin na 500,000, that's considered one transaction — binalik ko sa nag-deposit sa akin, that's another transaction. So magto-total ngayon 'yun na 1 million kasi may pumasok sa akin 500, may lumabas na 500." Buenaventura confirmed: "Tama po." 

Suntay also put on record that an impeachable officer can only be held accountable for actions during her term. 

He noted the AMLC report covered transactions going back to 2005, saying the panel had gone about 14 years beyond what should be the relevant period — which he argued should start from 2022, when VP Sara assumed office.

Focusing on 2022 to 2025, Suntay computed from the AMLC's own breakdown that approximately P60 million in transactions were recorded during those four years — P41 million in 2022, P4.7 million in 2023, P13.4 million in 2024, and P1 million in 2025. 

Buenaventura confirmed the figures were consistent with AMLC records, though he declined to compute the total on the spot.

data.text:
China published the energy coercion playbook for the Taiwan contingency on April 21, 2026, using the Philippines as the beta test. The same week, Japan landed combat troops on Philippine soil for the first time since 1945 to live-fire Type 88 anti-ship missiles. The coercion accelerated the lattice it was meant to prevent.

The signal is institutional. People’s Daily published an editorial titled “The Philippines should create conditions for deepening cooperation” under the pen name Zhong Sheng, a byline the Communist Party reserves for top-level foreign policy signaling. Reuters carried it under Joe Cash’s Beijing byline April 21, reporting Beijing implied energy assistance could be tied to Manila holding drills with the US and allies. The editorial accused Manila of hypocrisy for seeking emergency relief while hosting Balikatan 2026. “These blatantly contradictory words and deeds expose the opportunistic nature of Philippine politicians,” it read, calling on Manila to “create the right conditions” for cooperation. The subtext was legible to every Indo-Pacific energy ministry. China holds the world’s largest strategic oil inventories, imposed fertilizer export curbs after the Iran war, and resumed South China Sea oil and gas talks with Manila in late March. Three levers, one coded ask.

The structural vulnerability is arithmetic. The Philippines imports 98 percent of oil from the Middle East per DOE under Executive Order 110, signed by Marcos March 24, 2026, after Hormuz collapsed reserves from 55-57 days to 45 within three weeks. Diesel crossed 130 pesos per liter. Manila activated a 20 billion peso emergency fund from the Malampaya reserve, then secured 142,000 barrels from Japan, 329,000 from Malaysia, 320,000 from Singapore, 330,000 more to Davao April 24. Manila is diversifying, explicitly hedging against the supplier Beijing’s editorial just implied it could withhold.

The drills Manila refused to cancel are unprecedented. Balikatan 2026 runs April 20 to May 8 with over 17,000 troops from seven active nations, the largest in the exercise’s forty-one-year history. The US contributes approximately 10,000. Japan contributes approximately 1,400 combat personnel under the Reciprocal Access Agreement in force since September 2025, including Type 88 anti-ship missiles and the JS Ise helicopter carrier, firing Type 88 outside Japanese territory for the first time. Philippine Marines simulate-fire BrahMos. The most scrutinized drill sits on Itbayat, 155 kilometers from Taiwan. General Romeo Brawner told the opening rites, “Before, we were on opposite sides. This time, we find ourselves on the same side.” He addressed Japanese officers standing beside Filipino soldiers. The 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty marked its seventy-fifth anniversary the same month.

The mechanism is what matters. China is pressure-testing whether energy dependency can substitute for kinetic force in a Taiwan contingency. The Philippines is the experiment because 98 percent Middle East oil exposure makes the Hormuz shock readable as leverage Beijing never created but can now redirect. The 2012 Scarborough Shoal analog is instructive. Beijing tried economic pressure then. Manila pivoted toward Washington. In 2026, the pivot is architecture, not reflex. The Reciprocal Access Agreement entered force September 2025. The coalition assembled before the editorial. Beijing was reacting to a lattice already formed.

The falsifier is the fertilizer ship. If Chinese urea arrives in Manila ports through May without the drills stopping, the editorial was posturing. If it does not, it was doctrine. Either outcome is priced wrong today.

Hormuz is Clock Zero. It is generating every other clock.

Watch the fertilizer ships. Not the editorials.
